title: Karmic tail 15-20-5 in the destiny matrix: the “Rebel”, the reversed blessing and the liberty of service

seo.title: Karmic tail 15-20-5, the “Rebel”: meaning in the destiny matrix
seo.description: 15-20-5 is the most common karmic tail, found on one birth date in ten. A one-minute check, why Waite’s Devil is the Hierophant reversed, and rebellion vs freedom.

short: Popular destiny matrix readings call the 15-20-5 tail the “Rebel”. Here is how it reads. The entry is the Devil (15): a pull stronger than the rules takes hold of the person, and a ban only makes it hotter. The mechanism is Judgement (20): the moment someone else says “that’s not how it’s done”, the person rises up in an instant — argues, proves a point, slams the door, starts life over from scratch. The root is the Hierophant (5): the rule does not need to be defeated, and it does not need to be obeyed. What is needed is to choose an order you serve yourself, and to learn to say “yes” as firmly as you can say “no”. The tail’s whole path fits into three words: chain, call, vow. It is the most common of the 26 possible tails: it falls on about one birth date in ten since 1900. And everyone who has it has the same number at the centre of the chart — 10, the Wheel of Fortune.

sections.h2: Do you have the 15-20-5 tail? A one-minute check
paragraphs: You don’t need a calculator for this; three additions are enough. The 15-20-5 tail appears when the sum of the first three numbers of the matrix is **23, 32, 41 or 50**. A sum of exactly 5 also works, but only four dates since 1900 add up that way: 02.01.2000, 01.02.2000, 01.01.2001 and 01.01.2010. There are no other options.

ol: **Day.** A number from 1 to 22 is taken as it is; from 23 to 31, take the sum of its digits: 23 → 5, 27 → 9, 31 → 4.
**Month.** Its number: January is 1, December is 12.
**Year.** The sum of the digits of the year; if it is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1985 → 23 → 5, 1990 → 19, 1993 → 22.

paragraphs: Now add the three numbers together.

ul: 31.03.1993: 4 + 3 + 22 = 29 → not this one (this date has the 15-8-11 tail).

paragraphs: A sum of exactly **14** gives this tail’s “sister”, 6-20-14 (for example, 05.07.2000: 5 + 7 + 2). It has the same centre 10 and the same Judgement in the middle, but a different entry and root. How they differ is covered in the section on numerical neighbours.

Where this rule comes from. The bottom corner of the chart, D, is the reduced sum of the three numbers, and 23, 32, 41 and 50 all reduce to 5 in the same way. The centre E is the same sum plus D. That gives 28, 37, 46 or 55, and all four numbers have a digit sum of 10. The rest is fixed: the entry M = D + E = 5 + 10 = 15, the middle N = D + M = 5 + 15 = 20. Going through every day from 1900 to 2026 confirms that 15-20-5 cannot come about any other way.
This arithmetic also yields a few less obvious facts:

ul: **It is the most common tail.** 15-20-5 accounts for 10.1% of birth dates from 1900 to 2025 — first place out of 26, and first in every decade from the 1900s on. Among people born in the 20th century it falls on one day in ten (10.5%); among those born from 2000 to 2025, on one in twelve (8.4%), but even there the tail stays in first place.

**Why it comes first.** The sum of the three numbers usually lies between 20 and 50 (as it does for 87% of dates), and within this corridor four values at once lead to 5, with 32 sitting almost at the very peak of the distribution. Five is the most common number in the bottom corner of the chart. On top of that, all its sums give the same centre 10, so this whole stream flows into one tail. For six, which is almost as common, the stream splits between 18-6-6 and 9-15-6.
**Only two tails have centre 10.** 15-20-5 and its sister 6-20-14. The sister is almost ten times rarer: one date in 96.

**December beats January.** The higher the month number, the more often this tail appears: among people born in January it comes up in 8.6% of cases, in November and December in 11.1%. The month number is part of the sum, and high months find it easier to stretch it to 23 or 32.

**There are “bumper” years.** The tail appears most often in years with a large year arcanum, from 18 to 20: 1953, 1955, 1962, 1964, 1971, 1972, 1973, 1980, 1982, 1991 — 42 days in each of these years. Least often in 2000: 22 days.

paragraphs: Behind the name is a past-life legend that popular sites retell. The soul was supposedly born into a family with strict rules — noble, religious, hereditary — and rebelled. It rejected the faith or the craft of its ancestors, chose passion over duty, left of its own accord or was cast out. That, they say, explains today’s feeling of being the “black sheep” among your own people, the conflicts with parents and the pull towards the forbidden. None of this can be checked: you cannot reconstruct anyone’s past from a birth date. Besides, one person in ten has this tail. As biography the legend is doubtful. As metaphor it is precise, and it has support in the cards themselves — support of a firmness you rarely find.

**On Waite’s card, the Devil is the Hierophant turned inside out.** These are almost word for word the words of Arthur Edward Waite himself, who created the deck together with the artist Pamela Colman Smith. Describing the fifteenth card, he writes that the Devil’s raised right hand is **“the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card”**. Put the two cards side by side and you can see how one repeats the other. In the middle is a raised figure with the right hand lifted; below are two small figures. With the Hierophant they are two ministers kneeling before him, and crossed keys lie at his feet. With the Devil they are a man and a woman chained by the neck to a ring on the altar. Waite himself says this pair is “analogous” with the figures of the fifth card, and adds: “as if Adam and Eve after the Fall”. On the sixth card, the Lovers, he describes the same pair “as if Adam and Eve when they first occupied the paradise of the earthly body”, which is why the chained figures are often read as the Lovers after the Fall — the modern author Benebell Wen, for example, calls them exactly that. But in Waite’s description of the fifteenth card, the word is “fifth”.

**The legend of rebellion is written right into the description of the card.** Waite explains what the Devil really means: it is **“the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit”**. Breaking a commandment and ending up outside the gates is exactly the plot of the “Rebel”. Wen notices one more detail: the woman’s tail on the card ends in a cluster of fruit. It is a reminder of why the pair are now chained.

And now the twist that makes it worth looking at the cards and not just the legend. The Devil’s gesture is not an absence of blessing but its reverse, and the reverse has the same form: the hand is raised in the same way, only turned the other way round. A protest is a mirror copy of the rule it is aimed at. The Russian saying “I’ll let my ears freeze off to spite Mum” puts it better than any treatise: whoever acts out of spite is still letting Mum decide what they do — just with the sign reversed. Hence our reading of the name. The Rebel in 15-20-5 is not a person without rules. It is a person whose life is built around someone else’s rule with a minus sign. Freedom in this tail begins not with rebellion but with the moment the hand can bless again.

sections.h2: How the circle works: the forbidden fruit, someone else’s trumpet and a wheel without an axle
paragraphs: **1. Entry: the Devil — a pull that a ban sets alight.** Waite sees in the fifteenth card enslavement to the material and animal side of life: the chained figures have tails, the sign of the animal nature, but their faces remain human. Wen puts this into everyday language: attachment, temptation, the wish to have everything at once. She also links this card with “antagonism and dogma, despotism and enslavement”. In the 15-20-5 tail, the pull does not live on its own: it is lit by “you mustn’t”. A cigarette behind the garages at fourteen. A partner your family will never accept. A profession you were told “isn’t for you”. At forty — walking out of a “normal” job into nothing. Forbidden fruit is sweet not because of its taste but because it is forbidden.

Look at the card more closely. The chain lies around the neck in a loop, but both have their hands free. And the chain leads not to the forbidden fruit and not to each other but to the ring on the altar of the one who towers above them. In our reading this is the key detail of the entry: a person with this tail is tied not to the forbidden thing but to the ban. As long as there is a ban, there is a pull. Take away the “you mustn’t”, and many desires quietly disappear along with it.

**2. Mechanism: Judgement — a trumpet answered from outside.** In Waite, the twentieth card is not about punishment. The angel blows the trumpet, the dead rise from their tombs. The card registers **“the accomplishment of the great work of transformation in answer to the summons of the Supernal — which summons is heard and answered from within”**. Then Waite asks the reader: **“What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response — almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?”** Note “all that is lower in our nature” — exactly what the Devil card is about, the animal nature. Judgement is the card on which it rises to the call and is transformed.

In the 15-20-5 circle, the trumpet sounds from outside. It is Mum’s “when are you finally going to get your act together”, the boss’s “that’s not how we do things here”, a partner’s sigh, a stranger’s comment under a post. And “all that is lower” really does rise in the twinkling of an eye: hurt, anger, stubbornness, the urge to prove a point. Then comes a sharp turn: argue, slam the door, quit, move away, burn the bridges and start from zero. Each such turn feels like a resurrection. Wen writes of Judgement that the past, no matter how dark, is now behind you. And the person really does change position: in Waite’s divinatory list this card has “change of position, renewal, outcome”. But the direction of the new life was set by the voice they answered. It is not a call but a reaction to someone else’s trumpet.

The card’s Russian name, Sud — which also means “a court of law” — hints at another trap: judgement as a tribunal. A person with this tail can spend years conducting an inner trial: arguing with their father, justifying themselves to a teacher, proving something to an ex, although none of them has been around for a long time. But there is no judge on the card. No scales, no sword, nobody judging anybody — the scales and the sword belong to Justice, the eighth card. The angel does not hand down verdicts; he calls. The word “sentence” appears in Waite’s account of this card only among the reversed divinatory meanings, next to “deliberation” and “decision”. And Wen stresses that all the evidence is laid before the person, and the judgement is theirs to make. The mechanism of the circle lies in a double substitution: the call is replaced by a verdict, and one’s own judgement by someone else’s.

**3. Why the circle is so strong: the Wheel at the centre.** Everyone with 15-20-5 has 10 at the centre of the matrix. In the method, the centre of the chart is the comfort zone. In Waite, the Wheel of Fortune stands for “the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life”, and the sphinx on the wheel is the equilibrium within this motion. Waite even argues with pictures in which the sphinx lies on a separate fixed pedestal above the wheel: that way, he says, the essential idea is lost — **“stability amidst movement”**. This explains a lot for the tail. Change is home ground for these people, and a break-up doesn’t feel like a problem: “the wheel has turned”, “a new chapter”. The circle hides behind the romance of change and so goes unnoticed for a long time. But for Waite the point of the wheel is not the spinning but the balance that holds while everything turns. A wheel without an axle can only spin. The axle of this tail is its root, more on which below.

The arithmetic repeats this almost word for word. This tail’s Devil is made of the root and the centre (5 + 10 = 15): the pull is born where the rule meets the love of change. And Judgement is made of the rule and the pull (5 + 15 = 20). A coincidence of numbers proves nothing, but it describes the circle remarkably well.

**4. Root: the Hierophant — the blessing turned the right way.** In Waite, the Hierophant is the outer, established form of tradition: “the power of the keys”, the recognised hierarchy, **“the channel of grace belonging to the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature”**. In the historical part of the book, Waite mentions that this card was also called the Spiritual Father. He is in no hurry to idealise it: for him the Hierophant is the sum of theology “when it has passed into the utmost rigidity of expression”, although he is also all things righteous and sacred on the manifest side of life. And there is a danger: the pontiff may forget the significance of his symbolic state and act as if he himself contained everything his sign stands for. Wen sharpens the critical side even more. For her the Hierophant is both the pressure to conform and the habit of relying on an authority that will define for you what is right.

So the root task of 15-20-5 is not to go back to obedience, nor to finally find the “right church”. The task is to take the Hierophant’s place yourself. To choose what to serve. To set out your own rules and be able to explain why they are needed. To keep the form without mistaking it for the truth. And to bless — to say “yes” to what has stood the test: work, people, faith, your own family line.

Oddly enough, Waite put the formula for the way out into his description of the Devil. The one who towers over the chained pair, he says, is himself a bondsman: he is **“blind to the liberty of service”**. That is exactly what the Rebel cannot see: service can be free. The ministers on the fifth card kneel without chains. Waite’s divinatory list for the Hierophant begins with the words “marriage, alliance” and goes on with “captivity, servitude”. The same bond can turn out to be a vow or a captivity. The difference is one thing: whether you chose it yourself.

**5. Repetition.** If the root is not reached, after every break the person builds a new order. As it hardens, it becomes a new altar with a new ring. Yesterday’s rebel turns into a zealot of a new faith: a new teacher, a new circle, a new “only right” way to live. Then they rebel against that too. Or they start telling younger people, “When I was your age…”. Wen links the Devil with dogma and despotism, and this tail shows clearly how that happens: the anti-dogma hardens and becomes a dogma itself.
**Signs that the circle has started another turn:**

ul: you were told “you mustn’t” — and that is exactly what you wanted;
an argument is going on in your head with someone who isn’t there;
a decision is made to prove something, not because you want it;
you know exactly what you are against but struggle to say what you are for;
the thought “burn it all down and start again” comes before the thought “talk it over”;
you follow a rule — and store up anger at it.

sections.h2: A parable that reads like this tail
paragraphs: There is a story known even to people who have never opened the Gospels: the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32). The parallel with the tail is ours, not that of the method’s tradition or of Waite. But the match on three points is too exact to pass by.

The younger son takes his share of the inheritance, goes off “into a far country” and there “wasted his substance with riotous living”. That is the Devil. Then comes the moment the King James Version describes in five words: **“when he came to himself”**. The son hears a call from within, not from outside, and says: “I will arise and go to my father.” That is Judgement, and the parable even uses the same language: the father will later say that his son “was dead, and is alive again”. The father runs out to meet him and orders the best robe to be put on him and a ring on his hand. That is the Hierophant, the Spiritual Father, and his blessing. Even the ring is doubled here: on the Devil card, chains run from the ring on the altar to the necks, while in the parable the ring is put on the hand.

But there is a second son in the parable, and for this tail he is just as worth remembering. The elder son never left. When he hears about the feast, he “was angry, and would not go in”, and throws at his father: “Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment.” He served without freedom — he carried the chain as a duty. His father answers: **“Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.”** He had been free from the very start; he just didn’t know it.

15-20-5 has two faces, and these are they. The younger son is the open rebel who leaves, argues and breaks things off. The elder son is the quiet rebel who does everything as he should and keeps a tally of grievances for years. Both are chained to the same altar: one through “against”, the other through “must”. Neither has what Waite calls the liberty of service. The younger son thinks freedom means leaving. The elder son thinks service means slavery. The parable ends open: we never learn whether the elder brother went into the house. The root task of the tail lies in this open ending. You can only go in by yourself.
The entry and root of this tail are not two random cards but a pair that Waite drew as a mirror image. It helps to keep them side by side.

paragraphs: From outside they can be hard to tell apart: both the rebel and the keeper of tradition live by rules; the rebel’s rules are just “the other way round”. The difference is where the rule came from, and whether it can be explained without the words “that’s how it’s done” and “out of spite”.

sections.h2: Where else 5, 10, 15 and 20 appear in your chart
paragraphs: The numbers of this tail don’t stay in one corner. Since the centre and the bottom corner are the same for everyone who has it, so are the points calculated only from them. And where other numbers enter the calculation, the choice still narrows to two or three options. Here is what the charts of everyone with 15-20-5 have in common:

What everyone with 15-20-5 has

First number of the relationship line M–R1–R

paragraphs: **Purposes.** The options are this limited for a reason. Adding digits does not change the remainder after dividing by 9. For this tail, the sum of the first three numbers leaves a remainder of 5 when divided by 9, and all four purposes are calculated from the same A, B, C and D. That is why personal purpose here can only be 10 or 19, social 11 or 20, spiritual 3, 12 or 21, and planetary 5 or 14. A conclusion follows — ours, not the book’s. The Hierophant also appears in the planetary purpose of almost three quarters of the tail’s holders, and Judgement in the social purpose of more than half. What works as an argument with order in the tail ripens in the purpose into the ability to keep order alive and renew it. Arguing with the rule is a rough draft of the gift here, not an obstacle to it.

**Relationships.** Point M opens two triples at once: the tail and the relationship line M–R1–R. In 15-20-5 both begin with the Devil, so the tail’s scenario and the path to intimacy start from the same place. Hence one of its main scenes: love.

**The triple twice.** If you were born in 1906, 1915, 1924, 1933, 1942, 1951, 1960, 1969, 1978, 1987, 1996, 2005, 2014 or 2023 (a series in steps of nine years) and have 15-20-5, the same triple also stands on your relationship line — for example, for 05.11.1987. There it is no longer a karmic tail but a relationship programme, and it should be read according to the meaning of the line. But in such a chart the theme sounds louder than usual.

**The lower chakras and age.** All three numbers of the tail stand in the three lower chakras: the five in the energy of Muladhara, the fifteen in the energy of Svadhisthana, the twenty in the emotions of Manipura. So the tail’s theme also sounds in the most down-to-earth areas of the chart — support, joy and will. And the bottom corner D on the age scale covers the years from 60 to 70, and everyone with this tail has the Hierophant there — the role of the elder who passes things on. All of these are coincidences in the scheme, not a forecast and not information about health.
15-5-8 has the same entry; 6-20-14 has the same mechanism and the same centre. The fork lies in the sum of the first three numbers.

In 15-5-8 the Hierophant stands not at the root but in the mechanism: the rule there is not the task but what keeps the circle going, and the root becomes Justice — in Waite, a figure holding scales and a raised sword. In 6-20-14 Judgement and the Wheel are the same, but the entry is the Lovers, that is, choice, and the root is Temperance, the joining of two natures. In 15-20-5 the rule is not what holds you but what you have yet to build.
Below are typical scenes to illustrate the mechanism. They are not a portrait of everyone who has this tail.

A tail with the Hierophant at the root is easiest to recognise in relationships with parents. That makes sense: the first Spiritual Father in anyone’s life is the person who first told them what is right.

**Sunday lunch.** Mum asks in passing: “So what about work — are you just going to stay on that freelancing of yours?” The question isn’t even finished, and the answer is ready: “Mum, I’m forty.” Half an hour later the person leaves earlier than planned, keeps up the argument in their head all the way home, and once home decides not to come at all next time. They chose that work long ago, and chose it themselves. But at that moment they defend the choice as if they were making it again — and making it against Mum. The trumpet sounded from outside, and “all that is lower” rose exactly as Waite writes: in the twinkling of an eye.

**The elder brother.** Another person with the same tail has never once argued. They live near their parents, drive them to the country cottage at weekends, chose a profession and a partner that were approved. Inside, a tally is running: “nobody asked me”, “I did it for you…”. One day the bill is presented — in a row over something trivial, after which the person crosses out everything at once, or in a quiet coldness that lasts for years. This is the same tail: a chain worn as a duty.

Here it is worth remembering one of Wen’s observations about the Devil: the card does not mean the person is entirely to blame — much of the responsibility may lie elsewhere. For a tail about family this matters. Admitting your stubbornness does not mean admitting that all the grievances were made up.

**The worked-through version.** On Waite’s twentieth card, a man, a woman and, between them, their child rise from a tomb; the child stands with its back to us, facing the angel. In our reading, this is the best image for the worked-through tail. The family rises together, but each answers their own trumpet, and the child looks not at the parents but towards where the call comes from. Waite adds more figures to the family trio to illustrate “the insufficiency of current explanations”: even on this card, the family is not the whole picture. So a worked-through 15-20-5 does not demand going back under the parental roof, nor cutting ties. It demands something else: a grown-up chooses for themselves what to take from their family and can say so out loud. “From you I got my stubbornness and my love of working with my hands, and I’m glad of it. But this rule I’m leaving with you.” The blessing here goes both ways. The Rebel spends years waiting for the parents’ blessing or fighting for it. A person who has worked through the tail blesses where they came from themselves.
The point where this tail begins also opens the relationship line, so the circle is especially visible here.

**Forbidden fruit.** The strongest pull is towards people who “won’t be approved of”: someone much older or younger, of another faith, from a different background — an “unsuitable match”. The union rests on opposition: “us against the world”. And when the resistance vanishes — the parents come round, the obstacle goes away by itself — the passion somehow fades. The forbidden fruit has become just fruit.

**A partner in the Hierophant’s role.** The second scene starts later, in a calm relationship. Any request begins to sound like an order. “You promised to be home by eight” is heard as “you have to report to me”, and the person stays out late just to spite them. Bit by bit the partner turns into a parent, and love into an argument about who sets the rules here.

Compare two answers to the same phrase: “You promised to be home by eight.” In the shadow: “I don’t have to report to you by the hour.” In the worked-through version: “Yes, I did. I’m running late, I need to finish this. Let’s agree how I’ll let you know.” The difference is not submission. In the second answer the promise belongs again to the one who made it: “I promised”, not “they demand it of me”.

In its strong version, 15-20-5 has very loyal unions. Their rules were invented by the two of them and said out loud — “this is how we do it”, not “this is how it’s done”. Loyalty to what is imposed is hard for these people; loyalty to what they chose comes naturally. Waite’s divinatory list for the Hierophant begins with the words “marriage, alliance”, and in this tail a marriage becomes a vow when its rules are chosen, not inherited.

**Until the first “that’s how it’s done”.** In a new venture a person with this tail is often the best of all: the wheel at the centre, change their native element. The first months are bright. Then the structure hardens: sign-offs, reports, “this is how we do things here”. The old pull comes back — to leave, break everything, do it their own way. Their CV looks like a series of bright starts and abrupt exits.

**A church of your own.** The next step is a business of their own, “so that nobody tells me what to do”. A few years later its rules are stricter than the old boss’s ever were, and employees leave just as abruptly as the founder once left. The rebellion against someone else’s “that’s how it’s done” has ended in a “that’s how it’s done” of their own.

**Money as ransom.** Money easily becomes a ransom paid for freedom: earning so much that you don’t depend on anyone. The person works without days off for the sake of independence — and becomes dependent on work. In Waite, the Devil is the chain “of the material life”. Here it is worn in the guise of freedom.

**Where the combination works as a talent:** reform and launching new things, entrepreneurship, teaching and mentoring, methodology and standards, law — anything where rules need not only to be followed but also to be revised. Also public and religious work, and creative work that argues with the canon. These are directions, not a list of professions: the choice is still made by interests and skills. A person with a worked-through 15-20-5 sees before others which rules have already died, and knows how to offer living ones in their place without breaking everything around them.
The Hierophant is the card of the outer, established side of faith, so this scene is particularly visible in this tail.

**Changing churches.** A strict upbringing, religious or ideological. Then militant unbelief. Then a teacher or guru, disappointment, a new system. Each new faith is taken up with the fervour of a convert and dropped with the fervour of an apostate. The Hierophant’s place in such a life is never empty — it is just always taken by someone else.

**The matrix as a new Hierophant.** Even this article can become yet another authority for 15-20-5. “I have a rebel’s karma, something is wrong with me” is exactly the verdict the tail’s mechanism runs on. The tail is not a verdict. If you read it as an accusation, you are listening to someone else’s trumpet again.

**The worked-through version.** Beliefs — traditional or not — have been chosen and tested by one’s own experience, and the person can explain them without appealing to authority. They respect other people’s rules without submitting to them or fighting them. Wen, discussing the dark side of the Hierophant — the habit of deciding for others what they may know — puts it briefly: “We are not the keeper of others.” For the worked-through tail it is a good motto.

Among people born since 2000 this is also the most common tail: about one child in twelve. Usually it is a child who tests every “you mustn’t”. A ban without an explanation is a red rag to them, and “because I said so” is an invitation to war.

ul: **Fewer rules, but explained and firm.** A Hierophant without explanations is that very pontiff who forgot the meaning of his office.
**First acknowledge the wish, then say no:** “I understand how much you want it, and it’s still no.” A Devil that has been noticed pulls less hard than a Devil that was banned without a glance.

**Don’t turn a mistake into a trial.** “What happened, and how do we fix it?” instead of “You should be ashamed of yourself.” Shame is exactly the kind of outside trumpet the child will learn to rise to.
**Give them a say in some of the family rules.** A rule the child helped invent is one they will defend, not break.

**In teenage rebellion, don’t fight to win.** The father in the parable does not chase after his son or lock the door. He watches the road — and that is why he sees his son “when he was yet a great way off”.

paragraphs: Each of the four pairs below looks the same from outside but works in the opposite way. As long as you mix them up, the circle keeps turning by itself.

**Freedom or protest.** Protest knows what it is against; freedom knows what it is for. A simple test: if the person you are acting against suddenly said “great idea”, would you still want it? If the desire disappears along with the ban, it was a reversed blessing, not your desire.

**Call or verdict.** A call sounds from within and draws you forward — towards something. A verdict sounds in someone else’s voice and pushes you away — from something. After a call, you have the strength to act. After a verdict, you have the need to prove something.

**Renewal or escape.** Renewal carries the best out of the past; escape burns everything indiscriminately. The check is simple: after yet another “new chapter”, can you name what you took with you from the old one? If nothing, it was an escape, and the wheel has simply made one more turn.

**Vow or chain.** On the outside they are the same: you hold on to a job, a marriage, a faith, a rule. One question tells them apart — can you explain why you hold on without the words “that’s how it’s done” and without the words “out of spite”? If you can, it is a vow. If not, it is a chain, even if you put it on yourself.

sections.h2: The tail in shadow and in light
paragraphs: “Minus” and “plus” here are not two kinds of people but two ways of handling one and the same force: the pull, the ability to change abruptly and the need for order.

sections.h2: What to do with the 15-20-5 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: The exercises below were devised for this reading from the logic of the three cards. They are not a ritual and promise no result — they are ways to notice the circle earlier than usual.

ol: **The reversed-gesture test.** Before a big decision — quitting, moving, breaking up, starting something — ask yourself one question: “Would I want this if Mum (the boss, my ex, the community) said ‘yes’?” If you would, the decision is yours. If not, it is one more act of spite, and it is worth waiting.

**An audit of “you mustn’t”.** Write down the rules you live by or fight against. For each, make three columns: whose is it, why was it needed then, do you need it now. Some will turn out to be yours — keep them, but now as your own. Some will turn out to be someone else’s — let them go without a rebellion. A rule that no longer belongs to you does not have to be fought.

**A day before the break.** When you feel like slamming the door, give yourself twenty-four hours and one question: whose trumpet is this? A decision that survives a day can be carried out. A decision that rests only on a flare-up was an answer to someone else’s voice.

**One chosen vow.** Take on a small commitment for a clear period and keep it not because you “have to” but because you chose to: three months of classes, a weekly call, a regular task for someone. This is training in what Waite’s Devil cannot see — the liberty of service.

**Finish, don’t burn.** When you leave a job, a relationship or a community, close the door rather than slamming it: a last conversation, thanks, a list of what you are taking with you. In Waite’s divinatory list, Judgement has “renewal” and “outcome”. Renewal begins where there is something to take with you.

**Bless one thing.** Find one thing in your family, your faith or your former surroundings that you keep of your own free will, and say so out loud to the person it came from. The Hierophant of this tail is not the one who has received a blessing but the one who can give it.

**Your rules on paper.** Write down five to seven of your own rules and check each one: is it phrased as “for” or “against”? “I’ll never be like my father” is an “against” rule; your father is still in charge of it. Rewrite it as a “for” rule: “I explain to my children why.”

**Explain why.** When you are the one setting the rules — for children, a team, a partner — give the reason every time. This guards against the fate of the pontiff who forgot that he is only a representative. And against the day when someone close to you starts rebelling against you.

paragraphs: Change, if it begins, will be quiet. You argue less often and more briefly. The word “you mustn’t” prompts the question “why?” rather than an instant urge to break the rule. From past chapters you carry away people and skills, not just grievances. About your rules you have something to say besides what they are against. And in conversations with your parents a phrase appears that was never there before: “Thank you, I got this from you.”

sections.h2: The strong side: a person who gives rules back their meaning
paragraphs: In its worked-through version, 15-20-5 gives a rare combination. The Devil gives the strength of desire and the courage to go where you “mustn’t”, and so a knowledge of the forbidden from the inside — without moralising. Judgement gives the capacity for real renewal: these people know how to change their lives when life has truly run its course, not only when someone has hurt them. The Hierophant turns all this into a form that can be passed on: rules with an explanation, a living tradition, a teaching with room for questions.

Such people are called in when the old order has stopped working and a new one has not yet been invented. They are not afraid to say that the emperor has no clothes, and they don’t stop there — they suggest how to live from here. They know how to talk to people who have left home, because they left home themselves. And they won’t keep anyone else on the chain of “that’s how it’s done”, because they know how heavy it is.

Waite writes of the one who towers over the chained pair that he is “not to be their master for ever”. For 15-20-5 this line sounds not like a promise but like a direction. The Hierophant of this tail is not someone who never left. It is someone who left, understood why they left, and became a place others can come back to.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation.** Natalia Ladini’s scheme (points A–T): the bottom corner D is the sum of the day, month and year arcana, the centre E is the same sum plus D, then M = D + E and N = D + M; anything over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The rule “23, 32, 41 or 50” and the fixed points of the chart were checked by going through every day from 1900 to 2026. Frequencies, months, years and purposes were counted over all dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922, illustrations by Pamela Colman Smith) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations from both authors are given in their original English. Details of the pictures — the Devil’s gesture, the free hands of the chained figures, the Hierophant’s keys, the child with its back turned on the Judgement card — were checked against a scan of the 1922 edition.
**The parable of the prodigal son** — Gospel of Luke, 15:11–32, King James Version.

**The name “Rebel” and the past-life legend** come from popular interpretations of the destiny matrix. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or tails. The Devil’s gesture as “the reverse of that benediction” of the Hierophant, the driving out of those who ate the forbidden fruit, “the liberty of service” and the trumpet answered from within are Waite’s own points. Putting the three cards together into a scenario, reading the entry as attachment to the ban, the parallel with the parable, the tail’s two faces and the practices are the author’s interpretation.

**Limits.** The destiny matrix is an esoteric system with no scientific basis. A reading of the tail is a reason to take a closer look at your own repeating reactions, not a prediction, a diagnosis or a recommendation on health, money or relationships.

paragraphs: For a couple, 15-20-5 connects strong desires with the question of which rules to live by together. The Devil at M represents the pull of something deeply wanted; Judgement at N develops the task through relatives and inherited expectations; the Hierophant at D draws attention to agreements of your own and respect for differing beliefs. This connection is our interpretation based on Lisovskaya’s meanings for couples, rather than a reading of the triple supplied by her book.

Imagine partners who want a holiday alone together but routinely promise to attend a large family gathering. They may be tempted either to invent an excuse or to reject everything their relatives expect. In both cases, the decision still revolves around someone else’s permission. The combination becomes more constructive when the wish can be acknowledged without a secret bargain and the choice explained to relatives after the couple has agreed privately.

Choose one tradition and discuss what it means to each of you: what you want to keep and what you would change. Then formulate your own arrangement and each explain it to your own relatives, without making your partner the reason for declining. The difficulty is turning freedom from family pressure into a new lecture: “Only our way is right now.” The Hierophant as a task allows shared meaning to hold while making room for calm disagreement.

faq.q: What happened in the past life of a person with the 15-20-5 tail?
faq.a: Popular interpretations speak of rebellion: the soul supposedly broke with its family, faith or teacher, chose passion over duty, and left of its own accord or was cast out. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events in past lives — all the more so since one person in ten has this tail. It is more useful to read the legend as a description of what can already be seen now: the habit of answering someone else’s “you mustn’t” with a pull, and someone else’s voice with a break.

No, and in this scheme there is no 5-20-15 tail at all. The first place of a tail, point M, can only hold multiples of three: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21. The formula gives no tail that begins with five. If you come across “5-20-15”, it is either the same numbers in reverse order or a different calculation scheme. Here the tail is written strictly as M–N–D: entry, mechanism, root.

No heavier than the others. The most common tail cannot be a sentence: one person in ten carries it, and among them there are any number of calm, family-minded people who are quite content with life. The drama comes from the name and from the Devil at the entry. But even Waite, in the divinatory meaning of this card, adds that what is predestined “is not for this reason evil”. The difficulty of the tail is not an evil fate but a closed loop: rebellion and rule hold each other in place.

faq.q: Do I need to make peace with my parents?
faq.a: The tail demands neither reconciliation at any cost nor a break. Its demand is different: that decisions about family are made by you, not by your reaction to their voice. For some this will mean coming back; for others, a calm distance without war. The sign of a worked-through tail is not how often you see your family, but whether you can name what you took from them and thank them for it. If there was violence or danger in the family, your safety matters more than any scheme, this one included.

faq.q: Is 15-20-5 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. The calculation uses only the day, month and year. Arguing with the rule, the forbidden partner and changing churches are just as familiar to women as to men.

faq.q: Is the 15-20-5 tail linked to addiction?
faq.a: Popular interpretations often link this tail with a risk of addiction — because of the Devil at the entry. Wen does indeed list addiction among the meanings of this card. But a calculated number does not establish whether a person has an addiction and says nothing about their health. The loop “ban — relapse — self-condemnation — an even stricter ban” is familiar to many people without any matrix. If an addiction is real, it is a matter for a specialist, not for a chart.

faq.q: Why is 10 often written next to 15-20-5?
faq.a: Because everyone with this tail has 10, the Wheel of Fortune, at the centre of the chart — hence searches like “10 15 20 5”. The ten is not part of the tail but the centre, the comfort zone. It does explain, though, why the circle so easily takes the form of a “new chapter”: change is familiar to these people.

faq.q: Are the 15-20-5 tail and the “15-20-5 programme” the same thing?
faq.a: No. Only the M–N–D triple, running from the centre to the bottom corner of the chart, is called the tail. The same numbers can stand on the relationship line: for example, 31.03.1993 has the 15-8-11 tail and the relationship line 15-20-5. This happens for about one date in 37, and then it is a relationship programme, read according to the meaning of the line. And people born in the years of the series 1906, 1915, … 2014, 2023 who have this tail carry the triple in both places at once.

Your date of birth doesn’t change, so the triple stays with you. What changes is who runs the scenario: you or someone else’s trumpet. You can see it in small things: “you mustn’t” raises a question, not a pull; the arguments with absent people die down; you carry away something from old chapters besides grievances; your rules have an explanation; you can say “yes” as firmly as “no”.

report: “I’ll let my ears freeze off to spite Mum”: this Russian saying fits the 15-20-5 tail better than the legend behind its name, the “Rebel”. The legend says that in a past life the soul, born into a family with strict rules, rebelled: chose passion over duty, then left or was cast out. None of this can be checked. As metaphor, though, the legend is precise, and the cards themselves back it.

For Waite, the Devil is “the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit”. Breaking a commandment and landing outside the gates: that is the Rebel’s plot. His raised right hand, Waite says, is “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card” — and the Hierophant is this tail’s root. The Waite–Smith cards share one layout: a raised figure with a lifted hand above two figures, kneeling ministers on the Hierophant, a chained pair on the Devil.

The gesture is not an absence of blessing but its reverse: the same raised hand, turned the other way. A protest mirrors the rule it fights. Hence the saying: whoever acts out of spite still lets Mum decide what they do, only with the sign reversed. The Rebel of 15-20-5 is not a person without rules. **It is a person whose life is built around someone else’s rule with a minus sign.**

report.h3: Chained not to the fruit but to the ban

report: Here the Devil’s pull is lit by a ban. A cigarette behind the garages at fourteen. A partner the family will never accept: the union rests on “us against the world”, and once the parents come round, the passion somehow fades. Forbidden fruit has become just fruit.

Waite’s card shows why. The chain loops round the neck, the hands are free, and it runs not to the fruit, not to each other, but to a ring on the altar of the figure towering above. Our reading: **a person with this tail is tied not to the forbidden thing but to the ban.** Without the ban, many desires quietly vanish.

report.h3: No judge on the Judgement card

report: On Waite’s twentieth card an angel sounds the trumpet and the dead rise — not punishment but transformation “in answer to the summons of the Supernal — which summons is heard and answered from within”. Waite asks: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response — almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?” That lower nature is exactly what the Devil card depicts.

In 15-20-5 the trumpet sounds from outside: “time to grow up” from Mum, “that’s not how we do things here” from the boss. Everything lower rises in the twinkling of an eye — hurt, stubbornness, the urge to prove a point — and a sharp turn follows: slam the door, quit, start from zero. It feels like resurrection, but another voice set the new life’s direction.

The card’s Russian name, Sud, also means “court of law” — and hints at another trap: judgement as a tribunal. For years an argument runs in the head with a father, a teacher, an ex, all long out of the picture. Yet Waite’s card has no scales and no sword; those belong to Justice, the eighth card. The angel hands down no verdict; he calls, and the judgement, Wen stresses, is the person’s own. **The circle runs on a double substitution: a verdict replaces the call, and someone else’s judgement replaces one’s own.**

The centre of the chart holds the circle tightest: everyone with this tail has 10 there, the Wheel of Fortune, the comfort zone. A break feels less like a problem than “a new chapter”. But for Waite the wheel’s essential idea is “stability amidst movement”, and a wheel without an axle can only spin. Each new order hardens into a new altar with a new ring: yesterday’s rebel starts a business “so that nobody tells me what to do”, and within a few years its rules are stricter than the old boss’s.

report.h3: Two sons chained to the same altar

report: The parable of the prodigal son reads like this circle. The parallel is ours, not Waite’s or the method’s. The younger son “wasted his substance with riotous living” — the Devil. “When he came to himself”, he went home, and his father would say he “was dead, and is alive again” — Judgement. The father has a ring put on his hand — the Hierophant and his blessing.

The elder son never left. Hearing of the feast, he “was angry, and would not go in”: “Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment.” He carried the chain as a duty. His father answers: “Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.” These are the two faces of 15-20-5: the open rebel who argues and leaves, and the quiet one who does everything properly and nurses grievances for years. **Both are chained to the same altar: one through “against”, the other through “must”.** The parable never says whether the elder son went in. Nobody else can take that step.

report.h3: The way out is written into the Devil’s own description

report: The figure towering over the chained pair, Waite writes, is himself a bondsman, “blind to the liberty of service”. The ministers on Waite’s fifth card kneel without chains. The Hierophant’s divinatory list opens with “marriage, alliance” and goes on to “captivity, servitude”. One bond can be a vow or a captivity; the only difference is whether it was chosen.
The root’s task is neither a return to obedience nor a hunt for the “right church”, but taking the Hierophant’s place oneself: choosing what to serve and being able to explain one’s rules.

ul: Before a big decision, check whether the wish would survive a “yes” from Mum, the boss or an ex. A wish that vanishes with the ban is a reversed blessing.
Sort one’s rules into “for” and “against”. In “I will never be like my father”, the father is still in charge.
Find one thing to keep from the family line, faith or former surroundings, and say so out loud to the person it came from.

report: If there was violence or danger in the family, safety matters more than any scheme, this one included.

report.h3: The one who left and became a place to come back to

report: In the worked-through version, the Devil gives the courage to go where it is “not allowed” and an inside knowledge of the forbidden. Judgement gives the skill to change a life once it has truly run its course, not merely when hurt. The Hierophant gives a form that can be passed on: rules with reasons. Such people get called in when the old order has broken down and no new one exists yet. They will not hold anyone on the chain of “that’s how it’s done”: they know its weight.

Of the figure towering over the chained pair, Waite writes that he is “not to be their master for ever”. The Hierophant of this tail is not someone who never left. **It is someone who left, understood why they left, and became a place others can come back to.**
